issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'Being looked at sexually' is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision as the index trauma, especially when no other selected items suggest sexual trauma, harassment, or body-focused threat. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for signs that someone is entering the home implies an interpersonal intrusion/assault threat, which does not fit well with a motor vehicle collision and is not supported by the other items. The rest of the threat profile is general hypervigilance to sudden sounds, making this specific home-intruder monitoring item clinically mismatched.

issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes usually implies clothing cues tied to the trauma context. For a motor vehicle collision, this is difficult to justify unless other items indicate clothing-specific trauma reminders, which they do not. It also does not connect plausibly to the selected triggers, which are taste, workplace, and sexual objectification.

Workplace as a trigger is weakly grounded for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision given the rest of the profile: the other trigger and threat items are sensory/accident-related, but nothing in appraisals, threat, or strategies explains why the workplace itself would be a salient trauma cue. This makes the trigger set less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste linked to a motor vehicle collision is possible but clinically unusual, and here it is unsupported by memory content or appraisals that would make a gustatory cue understandable. With no memory items and otherwise sound/crash/vehicle-focused content, this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event

The rest of the triggers, threat items, and appraisals are centered on vehicle crash/sound danger, so these sensory triggers look clinically disconnected from the trauma representation described elsewhere.

Undereating as a coping strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and avoidance-based coping around crash-related distress; avoid-driving and screen escape fit that pattern, but food restriction addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, memory, or appraisals. In this profile it appears clinically mismatched rather than a coherent extension of the same trauma-linked cycle.

vignette:
Tariq's Collision

Tariq Nassar was thirty years old when the silver sedan ran the red light and struck his car broadside at the intersection of Fifth and Meridian. He remembered the sound first—not the impact itself, but the shriek of metal, the explosive percussion of the collision that seemed to come from everywhere at once. His left side took the full force. Glass showered across his lap. For a moment suspended in shock, he could not move, could not breathe, could only register the smell of spilled gasoline and something else, something acrid and chemical that he would later learn was the scent of the other driver's open bottle of whiskey, shattered across the pavement. The paramedics found him conscious but trembling, his left arm hanging at an angle that made his stomach turn. The other driver—a man in his fifties with bloodshot eyes—had been taken away in handcuffs.

Three months into his recovery, Tariq had returned to his job as a tax inspector, a position he had held for seven years with quiet competence. The work required precision, patience, and the kind of methodical attention that had always suited him. But something had shifted. His left arm had healed, though he still felt a phantom ache on humid mornings. What had not healed was the way his body now responded to the world. When a filing cabinet slammed in the office two weeks after his return, Tariq had flinched so violently that he knocked over his coffee. His supervisor had asked if he was all right. He had said yes, though he was not sure that was true anymore.

The avoidance had begun subtly. His ex-wife, Yasmin, had asked him to meet her for coffee to discuss their daughter's school enrollment. He had declined, citing work pressure, though his schedule was light. When his colleague Marcus offered him a ride to the airport for a training conference, Tariq invented a reason to take a taxi instead—then cancelled the taxi and drove himself, white-knuckling the steering wheel for forty minutes, his jaw clenched so tightly his teeth ached. He had not driven since the collision. The moment he turned the ignition key, his heart began to race. Every vehicle that approached from the side looked like it was going to hit him. Every red light felt like a trap. He had driven to the airport once and never again. Now he worked from home when possible, and when he could not, he took rideshare services, sitting in the back seat with his eyes closed, his phone in his hands, scrolling through games and news feeds to keep his mind from the sensation of the car moving around him.

The eating had stopped gradually. His mother had noticed first when he came to his parents' house for dinner and pushed food around his plate. He had no appetite, he told her. Stress from work. But it was more than that. Food felt like a distraction from the vigilance that had become his constant companion. His body was always listening now, always ready. He had learned to exist on coffee and the occasional sandwich eaten mechanically at his desk. He had lost twelve pounds. His clothes hung differently.

What frightened Tariq most was the certainty that had settled into his bones: he could no longer trust himself. The man who had once navigated complex tax codes with confidence now questioned every decision. When he made a minor error in a client file—a transposed number that he caught and corrected—he spent an hour convinced that he had made the same mistake elsewhere, that his mind was no longer reliable. He had come to believe that his competence, the thing that had defined him professionally and personally, had been shattered along with the windshield. Worse was the suspicion that he would never feel anything normally again. The world had taken on a flat, distant quality. His daughter's laugh, once his greatest joy, reached him now as though through water. He could not quite access the warmth that should have accompanied it.

It was his mother who finally insisted he see someone. She had found him one evening sitting in his car in the driveway, hands shaking, unable to go inside. That night, Tariq made an appointment. He was afraid of what help might mean—afraid that speaking about the collision would make it real in a new way, afraid that no one could fix what had broken. But he was more afraid of continuing as he was, trapped in a body that no longer felt like his own, waiting for the next sound that would send him back to that intersection, to the smell of whiskey and gasoline, to the moment when everything changed.
